rv.q: Mr. Hayes, who rose to fame as the flamboyant sidekick Jack in “Will & Grace,” here gives his finest stage performance to date.
'The Unknown' is an altogether sedate sit, sporadically livened up by the presence of its marquee star.
Yet as a theatrical mind game that leaves a mark or raises a shiver, The Unknown left me wanting.
But that sturdy sense of narrative determinism does shrink the play’s horizons, keep it packaged tightly, and make it consumable.
Hayes is always good company, but a thriller can only go so far into the familiar.
Expertly fashioned by some of the best storytellers working in the theater, The Unknown exposes our susceptibility to narrative, something that does not diminish with age and experience.
I'd pay to see a double bill of 'Harry Clarke' and 'The Unknown.'
While not fully successful in its narrative machinations, The Unknown proves intriguing from first moment to last.
But Hayes is wholly persuasive, shifting between an array of supporting characters with lightness and ease.
If the ending in particular made little sense to me, I'm not sure how much logically the rest of the play holds up under scrutiny either.
But instead of escalating, the play accumulates.
Hayes is captivating throughout, maintaining our sympathy even as his reliability as a narrator dissipates into mere wisps.
Cale has gifted him with the sort of vehicle he can return to for years to come, and it's easy to imagine that there will be a demand for it.
Hayes remains captivating, even if Cale's play meanders a bit in the brothers' backstory.
'The Unknown' earns its theatrical conceits through rigorous psychological honesty.
It’s primarily a well-crafted exercise that allows a beloved star to flex his acting muscles in front of his adoring fans.
